title: Interlanguage & Error Analysis at B1–B2

points.sub: A more complex system by now
pts: Interlanguage is the learner's own evolving linguistic system — neither the L1 nor the target language, but a structured system in its own right.
By B1–B2, this system has developed enough internal complexity to reveal genuinely systematic, rule-governed patterns.
This directly extends Unit 6's introduction of interlanguage into deeper analytical territory.

v: Five or six scripts from one learner

items: Gather five or six recent pieces of writing from one intermediate learner.
Underline every use of one grammatical area, correct and incorrect (for example, articles).
List the correct and incorrect uses in two columns.
Try to state the rule the learner seems to be following.
Plan one short activity that tests or extends that rule.
Do the same for two minutes of transcribed speech.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: One learner’s articles (written for this book):

lines: Correct: the sun, the Principal, a book, an apple.
Incorrect: I went to the market and bought vegetables. Vegetables were fresh. · She is doctor. · The honesty is important.

blocks.x: Learner’s apparent rule: use ‘the’ for things everyone knows and ‘a’ for countable things you first mention; leave out articles before jobs; use ‘the’ before abstract nouns because they are important. This is a coherent system that is partly right, and a teacher can work with it far more effectively than with a list of unconnected errors.

body: Purpose: to show interlanguage as a structured system between two languages. Content: two islands labelled ‘Home languages’ and ‘English’, with a third between them, ‘The learner’s English’, with its own roads and signposts and bridges to both. Style: map-like, clear labels. Board version: three circles with arrows.

items: Google Docs (free) with highlighting to mark instances by category.

blocks.x: Two coloured pens and the learner’s notebook.

pts: A systematic error reflects a consistent, if incorrect, rule the learner is currently applying — genuinely informative for teaching.
A random error is a one-off slip, not reflective of any underlying rule — informative mainly as a reminder that performance varies.
Distinguishing the two, as Unit 8 first introduced, becomes more analytically rich with the more complex patterns at this level.

items: Return a piece of writing with errors underlined but not corrected.
Learners try to correct each one on their own.
Those they can correct easily, they label ‘slip’.
Those they cannot correct, or ‘correct’ into another error, they label ‘rule to learn’.
Learners do the task in pairs, explaining their corrections to each other.
Support: give a code for each error (T = tense, A = article, WW = wrong word) as a hint.
Challenge: learners write the rule they think applies beside each item.

blocks.x: A learner’s sorting (written for this book):

lines: He go to school yesterday. → corrected at once to went: slip.
I have seen that film last week. → changed to I had seen: rule to learn.
If I will get marks, I will join science. → learner unsure: rule to learn.

blocks.x: Corder’s (1967) distinction between errors and mistakes is here turned into a learner activity. The ‘rule to learn’ lists, collected by the teacher, are the more useful for planning.

body: Purpose: to show the difference between systematic errors and random slips. Content: a learner sorting cards into two baskets: a small basket labelled ‘Slips: I can fix these’ and a larger one labelled ‘Rules to learn’. Style: friendly, simple. Board version: two boxes with headings.

items: None needed; this is a paper-based activity.

pts: A common systematic error pattern: applying a correct rule to cases where it doesn't actually apply (goed instead of went).
Overgeneralisation is evidence of active rule-formation, a sign of real grammatical processing, not simple carelessness.
Address it by contrasting the rule's actual scope explicitly, using consciousness-raising techniques from Unit 6.

v: Sets of examples showing a rule and its limits

items: Collect an overgeneralization from learners’ work, for example He suggested me to go.
Prepare a set of eight sentences: some where the pattern works (He asked me to go, She told me to wait) and some where it does not (He suggested that I go, He suggested going).
In pairs, learners sort the sentences into ‘works’ and ‘does not work’.
Learners try to state where the rule stops.
Learners write three sentences of their own and check them with a partner.
Use a corpus-based concordance of suggest printed on a sheet (Unit 58 develops corpus work).
Support: highlight the verbs in each sentence.
Challenge: learners find other verbs that behave like suggest.

blocks.x: Common overgeneralizations at B1–B2 (written for this book):

lines: He suggested me to go (from He asked me to go).
I am used to wake up early (from I used to wake up).
The news are good (from plural -s).
T: Look at ‘asked’, ‘told’, ‘wanted’. They all take ‘me to’. Now look at ‘suggested’. What’s different?
S1: After ‘suggested’ there is ‘that’ or ‘-ing’.
T: Exactly. So ‘me to’ is a good rule, but it stops at some verbs.

blocks.x: Overgeneralization shows that the learner has formed a rule (Richards 1971). Consciousness-raising, introduced in Unit 6, asks learners to find the rule’s limits rather than simply being told.

body: Purpose: to show a rule and its scope. Content: a field labelled ‘verb + me + to’ with verbs grazing inside (asked, told, wanted), a fence around it, and suggested standing outside the fence looking in. Style: playful. Board version: a box with verbs inside and one outside.

items: SKELL (free, from Sketch Engine) for simple example sentences from a corpus [VERIFY current availability].

blocks.x: Sentence strips cut from a photocopy.

body: Children acquiring English as their first language produce overgeneralizations such as goed and foots too. Such forms can appear after a period of correct use, producing what researchers describe as U-shaped development (Lightbown and Spada 2013). The same pattern in second language learners is a sign of rule-formation, not of forgetting.

pts: Unit 6 introduced fossilisation as a stable, resistant error pattern; at B1–B2, genuinely fossilised errors are increasingly likely.
Fossilised errors often need deliberate, explicit intervention — continued communicative exposure alone frequently isn't enough.
Identifying which recurring errors have genuinely fossilised, versus which are still developing, guides where to focus limited correction effort.

v: Error records for one class across at least two terms

items: From error logs (Unit 8) and marked work, list each learner’s most frequent errors.
For each, check: has it appeared for at least two terms? Has it survived correction and practice?
Mark errors meeting both conditions as ‘possibly fossilized’; others as ‘still developing’.
For ‘possibly fossilized’ errors, plan explicit intervention (see model language).
For ‘still developing’ errors, continue with normal feedback and communicative practice.
Compare lists with a colleague who teaches the same learners.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: An intervention for a stubborn error (I am having two sisters):

lines: Step 1: Show the learner a record of the error across three terms, without blame.
Step 2: Explain the contrast: ‘have’ for possession is not normally used in the progressive in standard British or American English.
Step 3: The learner marks every ‘have’ in one piece of writing each week.

blocks.x: Note that stative progressives such as I am having two sisters are common in Indian English (Sailaja 2009). Whether to intervene depends on the learner’s purpose, such as an international examination. Han (2004) warns against labelling errors ‘fossilized’ too early.

body: Purpose: to distinguish fossilized from developing errors. Content: error cards embedded like fossils in rock, labelled ‘Two terms, survives correction’, beside others on drifting leaves, labelled ‘Still changing’. Style: naturalistic, informative. Board version: two columns headed ‘stuck’ and ‘moving’.

items: Google Sheets (free) with one row per learner and one column per term.

blocks.x: An error record card for each learner, kept in the portfolio.

pts: Beginner L1 transfer errors are often obvious (word order, basic vocabulary); intermediate transfer errors are often more subtle — collocation, register, discourse structure.
This connects to Unit 33's genre and discourse awareness — transfer at this level often operates above the sentence level.
Awareness of a specific L1 group's typical transfer patterns supports more targeted, efficient correction.

v: Examples of collocation, register and discourse transfer

items: Give learners six sentences showing subtle transfer (see model language).
In groups, learners discuss: what would a speaker of your home language say here? Translate word for word.
Learners compare the literal translation with a natural English version.
Discuss which differences affect meaning, which affect tone, and which are Indian English features that communicate well locally.
Group learners by home language so that each group builds a transfer list for its language.
Support: provide the natural English version for learners to compare.
Challenge: learners find discourse transfer in their own letters.

blocks.x: Transfer at intermediate level (written for this book):

lines: Collocation: do a mistake (compare make a mistake); give an exam (widely used in India; take an exam internationally).
Register: Kindly do the needful in an email to a friend, where it sounds very formal.
Discourse: a formal letter that opens with a long paragraph of greetings and good wishes before stating its purpose.
Pragmatics: answering You didn’t finish? with Yes to mean ‘Yes, I didn’t finish’.
S1: In Kannada ‘yes’ here means ‘you are right’.
T: In English, ‘no’ goes with the negative fact: ‘No, I didn’t finish.’

blocks.x: Transfer at this level often works above the sentence, in genre and discourse structure (Unit 33). Swan and Smith (2001) describe typical difficulties for speakers of many first languages.

body: Purpose: to show that intermediate transfer is less visible. Content: an iceberg; above the water, obvious beginner errors (word order, basic vocabulary); below, larger areas labelled collocation, register, discourse structure and pragmatics. Style: clean diagram. Board version: a triangle with a waterline.

items: Google Translate (free) to compare literal and natural translations critically, never as an answer key.

blocks.x: A class transfer chart, one column per home language.

pts: Systematic error analysis across a class reveals shared patterns worth addressing at the whole-class level, not just individually.
This connects directly to Unit 8's error-log principle, scaled from an individual tool into class-wide diagnostic data.
Patterns identified this way should feed into unit and scheme-of-work planning (Units 11 and 14), not just isolated feedback moments.

v: One set of scripts from a whole class

items: Choose one writing task completed by the whole class.
Use a simple category list: tense, articles, prepositions, word choice, sentence structure, register, organization.
Tally errors by category (use a sample of fifteen scripts in very large classes).
Identify the two most frequent categories and the learners affected.
Enter the findings in your unit plan and scheme of work (Units 11 and 14).
Repeat the map each term to see how patterns change.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Class 9B, opinion paragraph (a fictional class, 48 scripts):

lines: Tense 41 · Articles 67 · Prepositions 38 · Word choice 22 · Sentence structure 19 · Register 9 · Organization 31

blocks.x: Decision: articles and organization lead. The next unit adds a ten-minute article clinic and a paragraph-structure focus. A class map is a practical version of the stages of error analysis described by Ellis and Barkhuizen (2005).

body: Purpose: to show class-wide diagnosis. Content: a bar chart of error categories with arrows from the tallest bars to a unit plan. Style: clear infographic with labelled bars. Board version: a tally table.

items: Google Sheets or Microsoft Excel (free online version) for tallies and a bar chart.

blocks.x: Tally marks in the teaching journal and a hand-drawn bar chart.

pts: An increase in errors during a complexity-focused task, per Unit 29's trilogy, may reflect ambitious new attempts rather than regression.
Distinguish errors emerging from stretching into new complexity from errors reflecting a stable, unresolved gap.
This nuance prevents mistaking productive risk-taking for a sign that a learner is struggling more than they actually are.

v: Two pieces of writing from one learner: one routine, one ambitious

items: Compare a learner’s routine piece (simple description) with a more complex task (argument or narrative with flashback).
Count errors in each, and note the structures attempted.
Ask: are the extra errors in the complex task in new structures, or in structures the learner already controls?
Classify each error as ‘stretching’ or ‘stable gap’.
Praise the attempt and target one stable gap.
Use recordings from a planned and an unplanned speaking task.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Two samples from one learner (written for this book):

lines: Routine: My village is small. There is a temple and a lake. People are kind. (no errors)
Ambitious: Although my village is small, but it has a lake which, if you visit in monsoon, you will see birds that they come from far away. (three errors)

blocks.x: The ambitious sentence has more errors, but it attempts subordination, a relative clause and a conditional. Although… but is a stable transfer gap from languages that mark both clauses; the extra they is a stretching error. Skehan’s (1998) accuracy–complexity trade-off (Unit 29) predicts this.

body: Purpose: to show that errors can signal ambition. Content: two climbers, one on a low, safe step, one reaching higher with a small slip labelled ‘complexity attempt’. Style: encouraging. Board version: two stick figures on steps of different heights.

items: A phone’s voice recorder for speaking samples.

blocks.x: Photocopied samples marked in two colours.

body: When a learner’s error count rises, look at what they were trying to do before you look at the errors. A page with more mistakes and more complex sentences may show more progress than a page with none.

pts: Systematic error analysis should directly inform the next unit's language-focus stage (Unit 28), not remain a purely descriptive record.
This connects the analytical work of this poster back to the practical, task-based teaching cycle at the heart of this tier.
Error analysis that doesn't change subsequent teaching has only done half its job.

v: The class error map (point 6); examples from learners’ own work (anonymized)

items: Choose the top category from the class error map.
Collect six anonymized sentences from learners’ own scripts, some correct and some not.
Plan the language-focus stage of the next task cycle (Unit 28) around them: learners notice, sort and correct.
Build the same structure into the next task so that learners use it in communication.
After the task, check the error map again for that category.
Learners write correct and incorrect examples for another group.
Support: the teacher provides the rule after learners have sorted the examples.
Challenge: learners explain the rule on a wall chart.

blocks.x: A language-focus stage built from a class map (written for this book):

lines: T: These sentences all come from your paragraphs last week. Some are correct, some aren’t. Which ones sound right?
I bought a book. Book was interesting.
I bought a book. The book was interesting.
She wants to become engineer.
She wants to become an engineer.
S1: The second one. Because we already know which book.
T: Good. And the fourth?
S2: ‘An engineer’. It’s a job, and it starts with a vowel sound.
T: Now describe your dream job and a book that changed you. Listen for your articles.

blocks.x: Error analysis that changes nothing next lesson has done half its job. Units 67 and 77 return to analysing learner language as research.

body: Purpose: to connect analysis and teaching. Content: a cycle with four stages: ‘Task’, ‘Collect errors’, ‘Map the class’ and ‘Language focus’, returning to ‘Task’, with a magnifying glass at the centre. Style: clean cycle diagram. Board version: a circle with four labels.

items: Google Slides (free) for displaying anonymized learner sentences.

blocks.x: Learner sentences copied onto the board without names.

body: Map one class’s writing task this week, choose the top category, and plan a fifteen-minute language focus from anonymized sentences. Map the next task and compare.

dek: Unit 49 of 100: revisiting Selinker's interlanguage framework from Tier I with the more complex, systematic error patterns that emerge once learners handle real complexity.

aims.x: By B1–B2, learners attempt longer texts, more complex structures and different registers, and their errors become more interesting: often systematic, sometimes stubborn, and increasingly rooted above the sentence. This unit returns to the idea of interlanguage, first met in Unit 6, and shows how to read intermediate errors as evidence of a developing system, and how to turn that reading into teaching.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain interlanguage as a rule-governed learner system in its own right;
distinguish systematic errors from random slips in intermediate learners’ work;
recognize overgeneralization as evidence of active rule-formation and respond with consciousness-raising;
judge which recurring errors are fossilized and which are still developing;
identify subtle L1 transfer in collocation, register and discourse structure;
carry out a class-wide error analysis and feed it into unit and scheme-of-work planning;
interpret a rise in errors during complex tasks as possible evidence of growth;
turn error analysis into a planned language-focus stage in the next unit.

why: Why this matters. Errors at this level are often more systematic and revealing than beginner errors — genuine windows into how a learner's internal grammar is currently organised.

background.x: In 1967 S. Pit Corder argued that learners’ errors are ‘significant’: they show the teacher what the learner has learnt, show the researcher how learning proceeds, and are a means by which the learner tests hypotheses about the language (Corder 1967). He distinguished errors, which reflect the learner’s current knowledge and recur systematically, from mistakes, which are performance slips that the learner could correct if asked. Five years later Larry Selinker (1972) gave the learner’s system a name: interlanguage, a language that is neither the first language nor the target language but a structured system with its own rules. Selinker identified processes that shape it, including transfer and overgeneralization, and introduced the idea of fossilization: the tendency of some features to stop developing even when the learner continues to receive input.

Jack C. Richards (1971) showed that many errors cannot be explained by the first language at all. Learners from very different language backgrounds produce the same intralingual errors, such as goed or He can sings, because they are working out English rules from English data. Rod Ellis and Gary Barkhuizen (2005) provide practical procedures for analysing learner language, and Carl James (1998) offers a detailed account for teachers. Zhaohong Han (2004) reviews the difficult question of fossilization and cautions that ‘fossilized’ is a judgement that needs evidence over time, not a label to attach after one lesson.

Indian classrooms add two important considerations. First, learners bring Kannada, Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Urdu and many other languages, often several, so transfer is multilingual rather than simply ‘L1 to L2’. Knowledge of these languages is a diagnostic resource, in the spirit of NEP 2020 and NCF 2023, which present home languages as assets (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). Second, some forms that look like errors against British or American norms are established features of Indian English (Sailaja 2009). The teacher decides which forms hinder communication or suit the learner’s purpose poorly, rather than treating every departure from a distant norm as an error. Unit 74 explores this pluricentric view of English more fully.

items: Single-learner analysis. A written account of one learner’s interlanguage rule in one grammatical area, with a planned activity.
Fossilization record. A two-term error record distinguishing ‘possibly fossilized’ from ‘still developing’ errors.
Class error map. A tallied map for one task, with the planning decisions it led to.
Language-focus plan. A lesson stage built from learners’ own sentences, with a before-and-after comparison.
Which errors in your learners’ work do you find most puzzling? Can you state the rule behind them?
How do you decide whether a form is an error or a feature of Indian English?
Which of your learners’ errors might be fossilized? What evidence do you have?
How do you know which home languages your learners bring to their English?
When did your error analysis last change what you planned for the next lesson?
How do you respond when a learner makes more errors because they are trying something harder?

terms.def: A systematic deviation from the target language that reflects a learner’s current knowledge, as distinct from a mistake, a slip the learner can correct. Errors show the learner’s developing system and are a natural part of learning.
The systematic study of learners’ errors, identifying, classifying and explaining them to understand the learner’s developing system and plan teaching (Corder 1967).
The persistence of certain errors in a learner’s language despite further exposure and teaching, such as a stable He go in an otherwise advanced speaker (Selinker 1972).
The developing language system of a second language learner, which has its own rules and differs from both the first language and the target language (Selinker 1972).
An error caused by the target language itself, such as overgeneralizing a rule (goed, childs), rather than by first-language influence (Richards 1971).
The influence of a learner’s first language on their use or learning of another language. It can help, as with shared vocabulary, or cause errors, as with word order.
A performance slip that a learner could correct if asked, as opposed to an error, which reflects the learner’s current knowledge of the language and recurs systematically (Corder 1967).
Applying a rule beyond its proper range, as in goed or childs; such errors show that a learner is actively building a system rather than simply copying.

A consistent deviation from the target language that reflects a learner’s current rule, as distinct from a random slip or mistake (Corder 1967). A learner who always writes ‘goed’ and ‘buyed’ is applying a rule.

A pattern in which learners use a form correctly, then produce errors, and later use it correctly again, such as went, then goed, then went. It signals rule formation, not forgetting (Lightbown and Spada 2013).
